intro: Every day the dice roll a premise and a dozen constraints, and the game has to honour all of them. Tonight's roll was seed 1706211053: a lemon who just moved in, brewing yarn balls, out of pride. Here is how that became a dye pot on the pavement of Vine Street.

rolls.value: a lemon who just moved in
rolls.became: The lemon at number 9 Vine Street, three days in. Mrs Marrow from number 7 has already said, over the wall, that lemons are “a bit sour”.

Natural dyeing really is brewing: you steep the wool in a hot pot of plant dye like tea. And lemon juice is the acid that makes many plant dyes take and brighten. The lemon is the one thing every dye pot needs, and it has plenty.
Balls of undyed wool, steeped one pot at a time and sold off a trestle on the pavement. More Wool puts more balls in every steep.
Hold the pot to steep. The shade deepens while you hold; let go in the just-right band. Too soon and it’s pale, too long and it stews to gravy.

Yards of yarn, from four to a hundred quadrillion: about what it takes to knit the whole Earth one layer of jumper. The pot grows to match, from a saucepan to a tin bath, a paddling pool, the duck pond, the reservoir and, finally, the bay.
Not to be liked, exactly: to prove a lemon isn’t sour. Every yard of bright yarn out there is the lemon’s answer to Mrs Marrow. There’s a doormat that says NOT SOUR.

Vi, the lime at number 11, watches over the fence and copies whatever you brew (lime juice is an acid too), and the Residents’ Committee clears the pavement after every Fair and takes the takings for the Street Fund.
Vi, the copycat lime, and Vine Street itself.
A dozen or so summers, each longer than the last. The kettles keep simmering at a low heat while you’re away, and the summer waits for you.

rolls.value: a forced reset on a timer; runs grow longer as you learn
rolls.became: Every summer ends at the Vine Street Fair, wherever you’ve got to. What you learn (a storm lantern, wellies, a cold frame, a pot cosy, hot water bottles) lets you keep steeping later into the year, so the summers grow from six minutes to twenty-one.
The chalkboard on the street: every colour has its own price a yard, and the street keeps changing its mind. A brand-new colour sells for double, until everyone’s seen it.

rolls.value: a recipe book: combine things to discover new ones
rolls.became: The Dye Chart: every pair of dyestuffs from the garden makes a colour, and you only find out which by steeping it. Woad and marigold make Lincoln Green; nettles and beetroot make Gravy. Each new plant adds a row.

Vi. Brew one colour for long enough and it turns up on her stall a penny cheaper, and its price sinks. The answer is to keep inventing, which is the dye chart’s job. A Taller Fence slows her down. She stands on a bucket.
The Big Cosy: a hundred quadrillion yards out in the world, knitted onto the gate, the house, the lampposts, the street, the town, the Downs, the clouds, the coast and then the Earth.

The Earth ends up in a jumper and it’s 41° in the shade. The porch thermometer pops. The whole street turns up at number 9 in shorts, and the big jug that’s sat on the windowsill all game is finally full of lemonade. “Not sour at all,” says Mrs Marrow. “Just right.” Vi starts knitting the Moon a hat.
A print cut in wood: black key lines, carved hatching for the sky and walls, flat blocks of ink. Everything the yarn reaches is printed in knitted stripes in the colours you’ve found.
Vinik’s muted, earthy 24 colours: exactly the colours natural dyes come out, so every square on the dye chart is one of them.
Mr Pepper at number 3 plays a steel pan he tuned himself, five notes only (A, B, C, E, F), and he says that’s plenty. The calypso uses his five notes, and so does every sound in the game.
Tea, wellies, hot water bottles, a cat on the stall and a committee with a clipboard. Nobody is ever really cross on Vine Street.

outro: A lemon, a dye pot and some yarn: it turns out that’s enough to knit a planet, if you hold on until it’s just right.
